doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Philly Joe Jones jam session and Hank Mobley's request
summary: At 16 he played at a Hampstead jam session run by Philly Joe Jones, who said he played like Joe Henderson; later Mobley wanted to borrow his tenor and he refused.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Very interesting story — there was a bass player in London called John Hart, who was part of, I believe he was part of the Woolworth family so at that time he was very well off and had a very large house in one of the best parts of London. And Philly Joe Jones came to live with him. It was extraordinary. I mean I think it was because there was access to drugs on the National Health you know. So he could register as an addict and he didn’t have to be hounded by the police or anything like that. But he took up residence in this house in Hampstead. And he couldn’t work because he didn’t have a permit, but he could teach and he could run jam sessions. So I got invited at the age of 16 to a jam session. And I’d been playing for three years and there were the best horn players in the country, all lining up, all trying to impress Philly Joe Jones. And we started playing a blues and it

got to me and I was panicking. I was going I can’t do a five chorus Coltrane impersonation you know, what am I going to do? Oh, I’ll play one note. I’ll play it again and add another one. Oh I’ll play it again, the third one, and then I’ll invert it — hang on a minute, this is what you do. And at the end of the number he came over to me and he said, “You play like Joe Henderson.” He ignored everybody else and came over — and I thought now I understand improvisation. Now I know what the musicality of being an improviser actually is, rather than oh I’ve got sixteen ways to get from a D major 7 to a G without playing every substitution in the book. So it was on-the-job. And as a coda to that, several years later, obviously on the advice of Philly Joe, Hank Mobley showed up in this house.

Me too. And I got a phone call from John Hart, who sadly we lost very young in a car crash. And he rang me and said, “Hank Mobley would like to borrow your tenor.” And I said oh. He said, “Yes, he’s arrived, he hasn’t brought one.” I said, “Oh what reeds and mouthpiece has he got?” And he said, “No he brought nothing, he wants the lot.” I said no. Not for me, and I passed.
You passed? I think I would too.
Well Ronnie Scott wound up lending him a horn you know, but in later years I told the story to Jimmy Heath and he said to me, “Oh you’d never have seen that again.”
It would have found its way to a pawn shop, ey?

Yes exactly. And he said, I won’t name the wonderful tenor player that Jimmy named but I’m sure you can guess who it was, he said he used to borrow my horn, I used to go to the gig, stand at the side of the stage and walk home with him.
